That is also true of a mistake: a key the editor does not know, or a binding pointing at a command that does not exist, is reported in the status bar as soon as you save. A typo that silently did nothing was indistinguishable from a broken feature, so it says so instead.

docs.title: Per-project settings
docs.text:
A .ase.conf beside your code applies to that project only. The nearest one at or above the file wins.

It may set only filetype.* — what a suffix means:

# .ase.conf in a C++ project that uses .h headers
filetype.h = cpp

It may not set build_command, lsp_command, or anything else that names a program to run. A repository you cloned writes this file, and opening a file in it should not be able to execute something. Anything else in it is ignored, and the editor tells you it was.

See ADR 0087.

docs.title: Colours
docs.text:
Nine colour keys, #RRGGBB or #RRGGBBAA. You rarely want to set them by hand — pick a theme instead, which sets all nine.

If you have set one by hand, a theme leaves it alone. A value you changed is a decision; a value still equal to what shipped is not, and a theme may replace it.

docs.title: Languages and servers
docs.text:
lsp_command = clangd              # any language without its own
lang.python.lsp = pylsp           # one language
lang.rust.lsp = rust-analyzer
filetype.h = cpp                  # what a suffix means

See Language servers.

docs.title: Build command
docs.text:
build_command = cmake --build build

:compile or Alt+B runs it and puts the output in a panel below the buffer. %f in the command is replaced with the current file, so gcc %f -o /tmp/a.out works on whatever you are looking at.

docs.title: Your first five minutes
docs.text:
ase path/to/file.c     # open a file
ase                    # reopen what you had last time

Launched with no file, ase reopens the session you closed — the same files, the same cursor positions. Launched with a file it opens that file and nothing else, because ase foo.c means foo.c, not "and the eleven things I had open last week."

docs.title: Vim mode is on
docs.text:
By default the editor starts in Normal mode. i starts typing, Esc goes back. If that is not what you want, one line in your config turns it off for good:

vim_mode = false

With it off, ase behaves like an ordinary editor: keys type, Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+Z undoes.

docs.title: The six keys worth knowing first
docs.text:
F1 Every shortcut, searchable. The same table this site generates from. : The command line — :w, :q, :theme. Also Alt+;. Ctrl+P Open any file in the project by name Alt+F Search the whole project Ctrl+W then a key Move between panes, resize them, close them Ctrl+S Save

F1 is the one to remember. It reads the same binding table the editor dispatches from, so it cannot tell you about a key that does not work.

docs.title: Your work survives a crash
docs.text:
Unsaved changes are snapshotted a moment after you stop typing, somewhere that is not beside your files. If the editor dies — or the machine does — the next start offers the work back.

That includes a buffer you never named. Ctrl+N, type, crash, and it is still offered when you come back.

Quitting normally is not a crash: work you were asked about and chose to drop is dropped.

docs.title: Where your settings live
docs.text: ~/.config/ase/config.ase, written for you on first run. :config opens it in the editor, and saving it applies immediately — there is no reload command and no restart. See Configuration.

docs.title: Try a theme
docs.text:
:theme
:theme simple-nord
:theme save

The first lists what is available, the second shows you one, the third keeps it. Nothing is written to your config until you say save.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Configuration — the file, and what it reloads
  • Keybindings — the scheme, and how to change it
  • Vim mode — what is implemented

docs.title: A prebuilt package
docs.text:
The alpha ships an AppImage, an Arch PKGBUILD and a .deb on the releases page. The AppImage needs nothing installed:

chmod +x ase-*.AppImage
./ase-*.AppImage

Each format is documented in packaging/README.md.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
You need CMake ≥ 3.20, a C11/C++20 compiler, and Qt6 (Widgets). The first configure fetches Lua, Tree-sitter and its grammars, so it needs network access; everything is cached afterwards.

git clone https://github.com/saeeedhany/ase.git
cd ase
cmake -B build -DASE_BUILD_GUI=ON -DASE_BUILD_TESTS=ON
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build

The binary is build/gui/ase_gui. cmake --install build puts it on your path along with a .desktop entry and an icon.

On Debian and Ubuntu the Qt dependency is qt6-base-dev.

docs.title: Which platforms
docs.text:
Linux. That is where the GUI is built, tested and packaged, and it is what a release is a release for.

The core library is built and tested on macOS and Windows in CI too, and the GUI has no deliberate Linux dependency — but it has never been built on either, so treat them as unverified rather than supported. On Windows there is a known gap beyond that: ase_process_spawn() is not implemented, so the language server and :compile are present and do nothing.

docs.title: Headless
docs.text:
The editing engine is a C library with no Qt dependency at all, and can be built on its own:

cmake -B build -DASE_BUILD_GUI=OFF
cmake --build build

That gives you core/ — the piece table, undo, config, the LSP client, the plugin host — without a GUI. See ADR 0002 for why the split exists.

-DASE_BUILD_GUI=ON requires -DASE_BUILD_SYNTAX=ON (the default). Turning syntax off while keeping the GUI on is not a supported combination.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Your first five minutes.

docs.title: Keybindings
docs.text:
Press F1 to see every shortcut, searchable. That panel reads the same table the editor dispatches from, so it cannot tell you about a key that does not work.

The full table is also on this site: Every default binding.

docs.title: The scheme
docs.text:
Chords are not handed out first-come-first-served. There are five layers, and which one a binding belongs to follows from what it does.

Layer What lives there bare keys Vim's language — dd, ciw, w. Nothing else may take a bare key. Ctrl+x What you bring from other editors and the OS: save, copy, paste, undo, find, quick-open. Plus Vim's own Ctrl+D/U/R/O/I. A closed set. Ctrl+W then a key Structure: regions, their focus, size and life. Vim's window prefix, with Vim's window keys. Alt+x This editor's own things — panels, pickers, tools. No convention to inherit, so a mnemonic letter. F<n> Ask the language server. F12 and Shift+F12 are what every editor uses.

The reasoning, and what it replaced, is ADR 0120.

docs.title: The Ctrl+W prefix
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+W alone and the status bar shows what it is waiting for:

Ctrl+W →  C  =  J  K  -  N  O  +  Q  W

j and k move focus between the buffer and the panel below it, w cycles, c closes whichever region has focus, + and - resize, o leaves only the editor. Escape cancels.

A prefix that swallows a keystroke and shows nothing is indistinguishable from a dropped key, which is why it tells you.

The prefix is caught application-wide rather than by the editor widget. The whole point is reaching the editor from the panel, and a key only the editor can hear cannot be the way back to it.

docs.title: Changing one
docs.text:
In your config, key.<chord> = <command>:

key.ctrl+s = editor.save
key.alt+g  = editor.find-in-project

The command names are listed in Every command. A binding pointing at a name that does not exist is reported in the status bar when you save the config — it does not fail silently.

docs.title: Only in one Vim mode
docs.text:
Put the mode before the chord:

key.normal.ctrl+d = vim.half-page-down
key.insert.ctrl+d = editor.cursor.add-next-occurrence

A mode-qualified binding beats an unqualified one, and your config beats the defaults — in that order. So you can rebind Ctrl+D everywhere without disturbing Vim's use of it, or the other way round.

docs.title: Two-chord sequences
docs.text:
> separates the halves:

key.ctrl+w>t = editor.compile

Not ., which is already the mode separator, and not ,, which is a key you might want to bind.

docs.title: Turning a default off
docs.text:
key.ctrl+d = none

none unbinds. For a sequence it unbinds that one continuation; the chord stays a prefix for the others.

docs.title: Writing a chord
docs.text:
Lowercase, + between parts, modifiers first: ctrl+shift+s, alt+left, f12, ctrl+w>j.

Punctuation is spelled out — semicolon, minus, plus, equal, comma, period, slash, backslash, apostrophe, bracketleft, bracketright, grave. Named keys are escape, tab, return, backspace, delete, space, left, right, up, down, home, end, pageup, pagedown, insert.

docs.title: Plugin commands
docs.text:
A command a plugin registered can be bound like any other:

key.alt+u = uppercase_all

See Writing a plugin.

docs.title: Language servers
docs.text:
ase speaks LSP over stdio. Point it at a server and you get diagnostics, completion, hover, go-to-definition, find-references and a document outline.

Linux and macOS only

The client spawns the server as a child process over stdio, and that path is not implemented on Windows — ase_process_spawn() returns nothing there, so the server never starts and :compile does nothing either. See ADR 0011, decision 6.

docs.title: Setting one up
docs.text:
lsp_command = clangd              # for any language without its own
lang.python.lsp = pylsp           # for one language
lang.rust.lsp = rust-analyzer
lang.go.lsp = gopls

The language id is the same name used for highlighting, so a language with no Tree-sitter grammar still gets a server.

The status bar names the server when it is running, and says so when it failed or is not configured. A blank bar read as broken, so it is never blank.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
F12 Go to definition (gd in Vim mode) Shift+F12 Every use of the symbol under the cursor Alt+S Outline of this file hover Hold still over a symbol completion As you type diagnostics Underlined, in the theme's own error and warning colours

Find-references and the document outline open the panel below the buffer. Ctrl+W j moves focus into it, Ctrl+J / Ctrl+K move through the results, Enter jumps — and keeps the keyboard in the panel, so you can walk a list of twenty references without reaching back for it each time.

Ctrl+O and Ctrl+I go back and forward through the jumps you made.

docs.title: Per project
docs.text:
One server per project per window, shared by every buffer in it, so opening a second file in the same repository does not start a second clangd.

The project root is the enclosing git checkout when there is one.

docs.title: Suffixes
docs.text:
If a suffix means something other than the default — .h in a C++ project, say — tell the project rather than your global config:

# .ase.conf at the root of the project
filetype.h = cpp

That file may only set filetype.*, never a command to run. See Configuration.

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin is one file you drop in a directory. There is no marketplace, no registry and no manifest.

~/.config/ase/plugins/

Everything in there is loaded at startup — .lua scripts and compiled .so / .dylib / .dll modules alike. A missing directory is not an error.

Both kinds register into the same named-command registry, so a Lua plugin and a native one are indistinguishable from the outside.

docs.title: Running one
docs.text:
:uppercase_all

Or bind it, exactly like a built-in command:

key.alt+u = uppercase_all

The editor checks bindings against the commands that actually exist — including the ones your plugins registered — so a binding at a name nothing provides is reported when you save your config.

docs.title: In Lua
docs.text:
One global table, ase:

  • ase.register_command(name, function(buffer) ... end)
  • ase.buffer_length(buffer)
  • ase.buffer_get_text(buffer, at, len)
  • ase.buffer_insert(buffer, at, text)
  • ase.buffer_delete(buffer, at, len)
-- ~/.config/ase/plugins/uppercase.lua
ase.register_command("uppercase_all", function(buf)
    local len = ase.buffer_length(buf)
    local text = ase.buffer_get_text(buf, 0, len)
    ase.buffer_delete(buf, 0, len)
    ase.buffer_insert(buf, 0, string.upper(text))
end)

That is a complete, working plugin.

docs.title: In C
docs.text:
Export exactly one symbol:

#include "ase/plugin_abi.h"

static void reverse_command(AseBuffer *buffer, void *user_data) {
    (void)user_data;
    size_t len = ase_buffer_length(buffer);
    if (len == 0) {
        return;
    }
    char *text = malloc(len);
    ase_buffer_get_text(buffer, 0, len, text);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < len / 2; i++) {
        char t = text[i];
        text[i] = text[len - 1 - i];
        text[len - 1 - i] = t;
    }
    ase_buffer_delete(buffer, 0, len);
    ase_buffer_insert(buffer, 0, text, len);
    free(text);
}

void ase_plugin_register(AsePluginHost *host, const AsePluginApi *api) {
    api->register_command(host, "native_reverse", reverse_command, NULL);
}

Build it as a shared module and drop it in the plugins directory.

A crashing native plugin crashes the editor. That is the inherent cost of native over Lua, not something this layer pretends to sandbox.

docs.title: What a plugin can do today
docs.text:
Read and change buffer text. That is the whole ABI:

void (*)(AseBuffer *buffer, void *user_data)

It cannot yet read or move the cursor, touch the selection, read config, draw anything, or react to an event. ADR 0009 deliberately shipped the smallest thing that worked, and the plan for widening it — an opaque context handle with accessors, rather than more function pointers — is written up in Extensibility.

docs.title: One thing to know
docs.text: Running a plugin command discards the undo history for that buffer. The plugin edits the buffer directly, underneath the undo stack, so the stack can no longer describe what happened. The buffer stays marked as modified so you cannot lose the file by accident, but you cannot u your way back past the plugin.

docs.title: Working examples
docs.text:
core/tests/fixtures/ has a complete Lua plugin and a complete native one, and core/tests/test_plugin_host.c shows how they are loaded and invoked. Both are real tests, so they cannot rot.

The design rationale is ADR 0009.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
A theme is nine colours: a background, a text colour, two syntax accents, a selection, a find match, a panel background, and an error and warning colour. That is the whole palette, deliberately — this editor's aesthetic is one background, one text colour and two accents, so a "simplified Nord" is Nord's ground, its text, and the two of its sixteen colours that pair.

Error and warning come from the palette too, so a Nord editor never flashes an Atom-red underline.

docs.title: Trying one
docs.text:
:theme                 list them; the current one is in [brackets]
:theme simple-nord     apply it now, nothing written
:theme save            keep it

Applying and saving go through the same code, so previewing a theme and keeping it produce the same screen. Nothing touches your config until :theme save, which writes a single theme = <name> line.

The built-in palettes are listed in Every config key.

docs.title: What a theme will not touch
docs.text:
A colour you set by hand in your config stays yours. The rule is that being in the file is not the same as having been chosen: a value still equal to what shipped is not a decision and a theme may replace it, but a value you actually changed wins over the theme.

This is worth stating because it was once wrong in the other direction. The starter config wrote all nine colours out, so every config file was full of values its owner had never picked — and treating those as choices made every theme a silent no-op. See ADR 0114.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text:
Set the nine keys in your config and leave theme unset:

background       = #1C1C1C
text             = #D0D0D0
selection        = #303030AA
find_match       = #3A3A3AAA
panel_background = #1C1C1CE6
syntax_type      = #87AFAF
syntax_string    = #D7AF87
diagnostic_error = #D75F5F
diagnostic_warning = #D7AF5F

Colours are #RRGGBB or #RRGGBBAA. The alpha channel is what makes the panels and the selection sit over the text rather than replacing it.

There is no theme file format and no theme directory — a theme is just those keys, so sharing one means sharing nine lines.

docs.title: Vim mode
docs.text:
On by default. vim_mode = false turns it off, and the editor then behaves like any other — keys type, Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+Z undoes.

This is not a full Vim. It is the subset that gets used, pinned by 218 conformance cases whose expected output was generated by running real vim, so where it differs from Vim that is a bug rather than a decision.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
Normal, Insert, Visual, Visual Line, Replace. The current one is in the bottom-left. Esc always goes back towards Normal.

A half-typed command shows in the status bar as you type it, so 2d sitting there waiting for a motion is visible rather than a key that seemingly did nothing.

docs.title: What is implemented
docs.text:
Motions — h j k l w W b B e E 0 ^ $ G gg f F t T ; , % { }, arrows, and counts on all of them.

Operators — d c y > <, each taking a motion or a count: d2w, 3dd, c$, >j. Doubling the operator takes the line: dd, cc, yy, >>.

Text objects — iw aw iW aW, and i/a with ( ) b, { } B, [ ], < >, ", ' and `. So ciw, da(, di{, yi".

Editing — x X r R s S J gJ ~ p P o O a A I i C D, and Ctrl+A / Ctrl+X to increment and decrement the number under the cursor. ~ toggles the case of the character under the cursor (and of the selection in Visual mode); it is not an operator, so there is no g~.

Registers — named "a to "z, uppercase to append. The unnamed register behaves as Vim's does.

Marks — ma to set, `a to jump exactly, 'a to jump to the line's first non-blank. Uppercase marks are global and name a file as well as a position.

Macros — qa to record, q to stop, @a to play, @@ to repeat. Counts work: 10@a.

Repeat — . repeats the last change, including after ciw, f, a macro, or a mark.

Search — / and ?, n and N, * and # for the word under the cursor.

Visual — v and V. Operators apply to the selection, and o swaps which end you are moving. r, J, ~, > and < work on it too.

Beyond Vim — gd goes to the definition under the cursor, using the language server rather than a local scan.

docs.title: The command line
docs.text: : opens it. See The command line for what it takes, including :s/from/to/ and :42 to jump to a line.

docs.title: What is not implemented
docs.text:
Blockwise visual (Ctrl+V), the case operators (gU, gu, g~), windows and splits as Vim has them (this editor's regions use Ctrl+W but are not Vim windows), folds, :g, registers beyond a–z and the unnamed one, and Vim's own scripting.

Vim-mode work stopped deliberately at the point where what remained was long-tail rather than daily. If something you use every day is missing, that is worth reporting.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Three tables, generated from the editor's own source every time these docs are built. They describe what the binary actually does, not a description of it that someone remembered to update.

  • Every command — every action the editor can be asked to perform, and the keys that reach it. Read from the command registry.
  • Every default binding — the built-in keyboard table in full. Read from keys::defaults(), the same table the editor dispatches from and the F1 panel displays.
  • Every config key — every setting, its default and what it means, plus the built-in themes. Read from the table in core/src/config.c that also produces the starter config file.

If you want to know why something is the way it is rather than what it is, that is what Decisions is for.

docs.title: Every command
docs.text:
Every action the editor can be asked to perform, under a name. These are the names the right-hand side of a key. setting takes — see Keybindings.

Each can also be typed on the : line — :editor.find — alongside the ex-commands listed in The command line. Both paths resolve a name the same way. See docs/adr/0128.

docs.title: Editor
docs.text:
Act on the buffer you are in.

Command Does Default keys editor.about About this editor Alt+I editor.command-line Open the command line Alt+; editor.compile Run the build command Alt+B editor.copy Copy Ctrl+C editor.cursor.add-next-occurrence Add a cursor at the next match Ctrl+D editor.cut Cut Ctrl+X editor.document-symbols Outline of this file Alt+S editor.find Find in this buffer Ctrl+F editor.find-in-project Find across the project Alt+F editor.find-references Every use of the symbol under the cursor Shift+F12 editor.font.larger Larger text Ctrl+=, Ctrl++ editor.font.reset Text back to the configured size Ctrl+0 editor.font.smaller Smaller text Ctrl+- editor.go-to-definition Go to definition F12 editor.help Show every keyboard shortcut F1 editor.jump-back Back to the previous jump Ctrl+O, Alt+Left editor.jump-forward Forward again Ctrl+I, Alt+Right editor.open Open a file Alt+O editor.open-in-project Open any file in the project by name Ctrl+P editor.output-panel Toggle the build output Alt+P editor.output-panel.shorter Give the editor more room Ctrl+W then - editor.output-panel.taller Give the output panel more room Ctrl+W then +, Ctrl+W then = editor.paste Paste the system clipboard Ctrl+V editor.quit Quit Ctrl+Q editor.redo Redo Ctrl+Shift+Z, Ctrl+R (normal), Ctrl+R (insert), Ctrl+R (visual) editor.replace Find and replace Ctrl+H editor.save Save the file Ctrl+S editor.save-as Save under a different name Ctrl+Shift+S editor.select-all Select the whole buffer Ctrl+A editor.undo Undo Ctrl+Z

docs.title: Vim
docs.text:
Bound in Normal and Visual mode only.

Command Does Default keys vim.half-page-down Half a screen down Ctrl+D (normal), Ctrl+D (visual) vim.half-page-up Half a screen up Ctrl+U (normal), Ctrl+U (visual) vim.number.decrement Subtract one from the next number Ctrl+X (normal) vim.number.increment Add one to the next number Ctrl+A (normal)

docs.title: Buffers
docs.text:
Act on the list of open files.

Command Does Default keys buffer.close Close this buffer — buffer.new New buffer Ctrl+N, Ctrl+W then N buffer.next Next buffer Ctrl+Tab buffer.previous Previous buffer Ctrl+Shift+Tab

docs.title: Panes
docs.text:
Act on the regions of the window.

Command Does Default keys pane.close Close the focused region Ctrl+W then C, Ctrl+W then Q pane.cycle Cycle between regions Ctrl+W then W pane.focus-down Focus the region below Ctrl+W then J pane.focus-up Focus the region above Ctrl+W then K pane.only Close everything but the editor Ctrl+W then O

docs.title: Every config key
docs.text:
One key = value per line in ~/.config/ase/config.ase. See Configuration for the file's shape and how it reloads.

A key written <like this> stands for a family: substitute the part in angle brackets.

A key marked project can also be set in a .ase.conf at the root of a project, which only that project reads.

Key Default Means Project background #282828 Page colour. #RRGGBB or #RRGGBBAA. — text #F5E6C8 Text colour. — selection #45403866 Selection highlight. — find_match #45403899 The current find/replace match. — panel_background #282828E6 Floating panels (find, open, help). — diagnostic_error #E06C75 Language-server error underline. — diagnostic_warning #E5C07B Language-server warning underline. — syntax_type #689d6a Types. One of only two syntax colours. — syntax_string #d79921 String literals. The other one. — font_family monospace Editor font. — font_size 11 Point size. Ctrl+= / Ctrl+- override it live. — vim_mode true Modal editing. false for always-insert. — animations false true for a smooth caret fade instead of a blink. — line_numbers absolute off, absolute, or relative. — theme ase-default Colour palette. :theme lists them. — max_fps unset Cap the animation rate; unset follows the display. — build_command unset :compile runs this; %f is the current file. — lsp_command unset Language server for any language without its own. — syntax_max_kb 1024 Skip highlighting past this file size, in KB. — restore_session true Reopen last session's files when started bare. — git_marks true Gutter bars for lines changed since the last commit. — key.<chord> unset Run a command on a chord, e.g. key.ctrl+s = editor.save. — lang.<id>.lsp unset Language server for one language, e.g. lang.cpp.lsp. — filetype.<suffix> unset What a suffix means, e.g. filetype.h = cpp. yes
